heldBackBy.answer: Mostly the game's own structure: no scholarship, a local grad, and I refused shortcuts and padded nothing, so I never got the visible big wins. I did reach Minister at 70 though, so I am not sure anything was held back. Deferring the overseas posting in Y23 and never being re-offered it probably cost me the most.

Nothing really did. Integrity and reputation stayed near 100 all the way, so the run felt like a smooth escalator. My career was held back only by the lack of a scholarship early on, and the game barely made that matter.

Honestly, nothing held me back much; I ended as DPM with INTEG 100. The only drag was STAND, which dipped when I was honest in public, and that matches how real careers work. I suspect the game rewards plain sensible play and does not punish integrity enough.
I had no scholarship, so I was never on the fast track. Candour cost me a little standing, and I got there anyway, just later than the scholars. The Harvard slots going to juniors twice fits that.

Visibility. I was honest and competent but never played the reputation game, so REP stayed at 50 while INTEG and COMP were maxed out. The game seems to say that being clean is not enough without being seen.

My own habit of being honest when silence would have been safer, plus the CEP line heard as 'well, realistically' in Y13. I never got onto the Leadership Programme list in Y40, and falling STAND meant I was never seen as political material.

Mostly the REP stat. I stayed at 51 while INTEG and COMP were maxed, so I was clean and competent but not known. In the end the ward result was about the team and the party, not me, as the card said. The game seems to reward visibility over integrity.

Probably never being a scholar, plus being too candid for too long. STAND kept sliding, so I think candour costs standing with those above, and a backbench ending suggests nobody ever saw me as portfolio material. The game never told me which it was.

best.what: Became DPM at MOF and the townhall workload question was read aloud, giving a STAND bump. It felt like honesty paying off in a way the system actually noticed.

worst.what: The quiet years at DPM level (44-46) repeated the same fix-something or PQ choices with nothing new landing. It was a long flat stretch before the end.

skip.why: A quiet year where nothing happened and the only choice was to rest. It added nothing to read or decide.

diaries.fair: Retiring as DPM with integrity 100 and a line saying the system carried on without me is exactly how a real career ends. It was dry and a little deflating, which is true to life. The unresolved threads (lift audit, stallholder) bothered me, though.
diaries.again: The middle and late years got repetitive, with the same PQ and MPS events and little variety. I'd want some time away, though the early-career detail was good enough that I might return.

best.what: The Town Council lift contract with the contractor's cousin, where I chose the proper slow process. It felt like a real insider dilemma, and I wanted to see if the accounts would vindicate me.

worst.what: A recycled quiet-year event, the same 'fix something nobody asked for' choice as Y45. It felt like filler, and nothing came back from either fix.

skip.why: It was the fourth PQ with an unflattering honest answer, and I had already seen the pattern. Being left off the Leadership Programme list with no reason given was the only new thing, and it was barely explored.

diaries.fair: The decline in standing followed from my choices and I could trace it. 'Retired, Honourably' is also how a long and unremarkable career ends. Reaching DPM on the strength of candour alone is generous, but the ending itself was fair.
diaries.again: The middle years recycled events too much and my choices felt like the same ones repeated. I would need a break, and a reason to expect different events.

best.what: Writing eleven argued appeal letters at the MPS and seeing three succeed. It felt like real work with a small, believable payoff, not a big reward.

worst.what: The same PQ event appearing again with the same choices, and STAND dropping after another straight answer. It felt repetitive, and the game seemed to punish honesty without telling me why.

skip.why: A repeat of the Y45 event, with nothing new to decide and a quiet standing loss at the end.

diaries.fair: Retiring honourably at 72 with integrity 100 is about what a careful, honest officer would get. The card's line that the service continued, unremarkably, is the sort of thing an insider would say and be right about. I only wish the dormant company folder and the lift contractor had come back.
diaries.again: The clean run was consistent but a bit flat in the later decades, with repeated events and loose threads. I'd come back later, and only for a different kind of life.

best.what: Nominating the quiet officer for PSLP instead of myself, then having her quietly put my name forward in Y12. It felt like how favours really travel in the service: unspoken and years later.

worst.what: The second workload Townhall, which was a repeat of Y33 with a STAND change of -1. By then the loop of Townhall, fix something nobody asked for and PQ answer had gone flat.

skip.why: A quiet year where I repeated a choice I had already made and nothing new happened. I could have tapped straight through.

diaries.fair: I reached PM with Integrity 100 after mostly sensible and occasionally principled choices, and the card said the formula was published so nobody could say they were not told. That fits the real system. I never saw the Y4 consultants choice or the Y29 Cabinet question pay off, though, so some threads just stopped.
diaries.again: The middle and late years got repetitive, with the same PQ and Townhall beats, and I would want a break before trying a different temperament.

best.what: Asking in Cabinet whether ministers should be paid on indicators they set, and watching STAND fall from 68 to 54. It was the one time the game made a principled choice cost something visible, and it felt like a real insider moment.

worst.what: The run of quiet years (Y41, Y44, Y46) where I tapped A and fixed an unasked thing. The same 'wider responsibility' appraisal and door-facing seat rumour kept repeating, so nothing landed.

skip.why: A quiet year with no real decision. It was the same beat as Y44 and Y46, and I could have gone straight from the Leadership list snub to the next real event.

diaries.fair: It matched how the service works: a clean, long career with no scandal, an unremarkable exit and no explanation for the snubs. The lifetime earnings number was a nice dry touch. I would have liked one line explaining the Leadership list, but not having it is also true to life.
diaries.again: The first twenty years were interesting, but the last decade was too repetitive. I would come back after a break and take a different path.

best.what: Asking in Cabinet whether ministers should be paid on indicators they set. It was minuted and left unanswered, which is exactly what would happen in real life, and it made me laugh.

worst.what: The quiet year where I fixed something nobody asked for. It was flat, and the events repeated by then (Townhall workload, MPS case), so the late game felt like tapping through the same few cards.

skip.why: It was a repeat of the Y43 Townhall workload question, same choice and same outcome, with nothing new to decide.

diaries.fair: 'Served, the service continued' is a very accurate and very Singapore line. DPM at 72 with a clean record matches how I played. I did not become PM, but I never chased it.
diaries.again: Not right now. 46 years is long, and events repeat so much that I think I have seen most of it. Maybe later with a different temperament, as a corner-cutter.

best.what: The quiet officer I nominated back in Y2 came back as Deputy Secretary and put my name forward unasked. It was the one callback that felt like how the service really works: people remember who backed them.

worst.what: Writing appeal letters properly for the second year running. It was the same choice with the same closed-case man, and nothing new landed.

skip.why: It was a near-repeat of Y31 with no new information. The Y31 to Y34 stretch blurred together.

diaries.fair: I made the choices I would have made, and PM at 59 with integrity at 100 matches them. The earnings line was blunt, but it was honest about the published formula.
diaries.again: It was a decent run, but the middle years were repetitive and I know roughly how it goes. I would come back later for the civil service-only path.

best.what: Vetting for politics: I disclosed everything including the dormant company and the folder, and the candour actually helped. It was the first time the game rewarded the dull, correct choice, and that is how it feels in the real service.

worst.what: A quiet year where I fixed something nobody asked for and STAND just dropped 2. Nothing to chew on, and it felt like the game was filling time near the end.

skip.why: The MPS nights repeated for decades with the same appeal-letter choice. Once I had picked the proper route, later years in that run added nothing.

diaries.fair: DPM, retired honourably, integrity 100, matches the life I played. I never became PM, and given the choices I made, third column is exactly where a system like this would keep me. Several threads I was watching (cousin, dormant company, folder, appeal man) never visibly paid off, which was a little disappointing.
diaries.again: The run was 70-odd years of mostly similar tap choices, and I've seen the main loop. I'd come back another day for the compromise run, not straight away.

best.what: Reading out the workload question at the townhall and answering it straight; STAND went to 89 the next year. It was the one time candour visibly paid off.

worst.what: Conceding the scheme point on Facebook at 11pm and watching STAND drop 8. It felt like being punished for the honest choice, and the game never really explained why.

skip.why: Not on the Leadership Programme list with no reason given. Realistic, but nothing to play. I just absorbed it and moved on.

diaries.fair: DPM at 72 with Integrity 100 matches how I played. The card's line about being unremarkable is exactly how the service sees a good career. I wanted the dangling threads resolved, though.
diaries.again: Forty-odd years of taps is a lot, and many of my choices felt the same. I would come back later with a different plan, not straight away.

best.what: Laughing off the political approach and having it pay off later. It felt true to how the service works, where the offer comes sideways and you can only decline gracefully.

worst.what: The Townhall repeated the rude workload question I had already answered in Y42. It felt like a recycled event, and my notes show STAND was already sliding with no clear way to recover it.

skip.why: The director fishing for 'system is a joke' was a discretion test I never saw resolved. I said nothing and got no payoff, so the year felt like a setup with no follow-through.

diaries.fair: Yes. Backbench lifer with full integrity and people coming to say thanks fits how I played. I traded standing for being straight, and it is a decent ending, though the line about the queue out the door was a bit sentimental.
diaries.again: Not right now. The run was long and the later decades blurred together. I would come back for a different path, but not straight away.

best.what: Conceding on Facebook at 11pm and being made Minister MR4. It felt like a believable mix of a small act of candour and real career consequences.

worst.what: Seeing every last resident at Tuesday MPS and then watching STAND fall anyway. The repeated PQ and walkabout years blurred together and the feedback contradicted my choices.

skip.why: Another sharp PQ, answered straight again. It was the same beat as Y31 with the same unexplained STAND drift, and nothing new landed.

diaries.fair: Candour and trust-building paid off throughout, and the formula was stated on the card. The ending matched my choices, though the STAND decline never resolved and the Y3 pilot and the Tuesday man never visibly came back, which left loose ends.
diaries.again: The late years repeated themselves and the clear rule was candour pays. I would come back after a break to try a worse-behaved career, not right now.

best.what: Giving the honest PQ answer even though STAND fell to 71 and there was blowback. It felt like a real civil-service-turned-politician dilemma, and the cost was believable.

worst.what: The director baiting me with 'this system is a joke, isn't it?' and my silence. The game felt like it was winking at me, and nothing visible followed from the choice.

skip.why: The rude workload question at the townhall had repeated by then and the outcome was predictable. Odd-year chilli stallholder years also blurred together.

diaries.fair: Retiring honourably as DPM with Integrity 100 matches how I played, and the card's line about being unremarkable is exactly the highest compliment the system gives. Several promised payoffs never arrived, though.
diaries.again: The institutional detail was good, but nearly fifty years of one-tap years got repetitive, and too many threads I kept in my notes never paid off. I would want some time before another run.

best.what: Maiden speech with one true thing in it, and an unknown Minister sending 'That needed saying.' Small, quiet and exactly how it happens in real life.

worst.what: The same PQ event a third time running, and I answered straight again. It felt like the game had run out of ideas for mid-career years, and the STAND drops were just a number going down.

skip.why: Another MPS where I saw every resident, and the weekly man with the closed case never came back. Nothing new happened, so I would have tapped straight through.

diaries.fair: DPM with integrity 100 matches how I played, and the retirement card is dry and accurate. I would have liked some acknowledgement of the cost to family, since I missed the concert and nothing ever came of it.
diaries.again: The middle decades repeated too much and I mostly knew what I would pick. I would wait a while and try a different temperament later.

best.what: Listening to the chilli stallholder on camera and watching STAND recover. It was the one time a small human choice visibly paid off, and it felt true to how a walkabout actually works.

worst.what: The fourth walkabout with the chilli stallholder. By then the repeat was tedious, and STAND kept sliding whatever I chose, so the choice felt decorative.

skip.why: Same walkabout and same stallholder as the years either side, with no new information and a small STAND drop. It could have been folded into one beat.

diaries.fair: A cautious, honest, competent officer reaching the top feels plausible, and the card's line that the formula was published is a sharp, accurate jab. But the run felt too smooth, since nothing I did ever truly blocked me.
diaries.again: The institutional details were good, but the late years repeated events and my choices did not seem to change the outcome. I would wait a while, or try it only to see a failure path.

best.what: Asking in Cabinet whether ministers should be paid on indicators they set. STAND dropped to 31 and later rebounded. It was the only choice that felt like something an insider would actually dread doing, and it had a real cost.

worst.what: The townhall workload question again. It was the fifth time I read out the upvoted question, and I was told to commit to a dated action that the game never really let me take or pay off. It felt like a loop.

skip.why: Not on the Leadership Programme list, no reason given. It's realistic, but it led nowhere I could act on. I wanted an appeal path and only got one two years later.

diaries.fair: I ended as a Minister with Integrity at 100 and a long career. The card's line about being unremarkable is exactly the kind of accurate, dry compliment the service gives. I'd have liked a nod to the unresolved workload promise.
diaries.again: It was a long run with a lot of repeated townhall and MPS beats. I'd come back later with a different strategy, but not right now.

best.what: The townhall where I answered the rude question straight and STAND recovered. It was the one time honesty paid off visibly in the game.

worst.what: The MPS appeal letters for the same man again, plus the Harvard rumour again. By then the events were plainly recycling and nothing I chose changed anything.

skip.why: The wet market chillies walkabout, repeated in Y46. I was waiting for the Y24 stallholder to come back and got a copy of an ordinary event.

diaries.fair: Retiring as DPM with integrity 100 matches how I played, and the line about the service continuing is accurate and made me smile. But the ending reflects my pattern more than any particular choice, so it felt a bit generic.
diaries.again: The late game recycled too much, and I suspect another honest run would show me the same events. I would come back if I heard the events had been expanded.
